examples.question_text:
Two cricket players' scores last season are summarised below.

$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Player}&\textbf{Mean runs}&\textbf{Range of runs}\\\hline\text{Amira}&46&18\\\text{Theo}&53&31\end{array}$

Compare their performances using both statistics. Does either player have the better result on both measures?
examples.solution_text:
$53>46$
Theo scored more runs per innings on average because his mean is higher.

$18<31$
Amira was more consistent because her scores have the smaller range.

Neither player has the better result on both measures: Theo scored more on average, while Amira was more consistent.

examples.question_text:
The table summarises a class's test marks in three subjects.

$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Subject}&\textbf{Median mark}&\textbf{Range of marks}\\\hline\text{English}&64&30\\\text{Maths}&71&38\\\text{Science}&67&16\end{array}$

In which subject did students do best, according to the median? In which subject were their marks most similar? Explain using the statistics.
examples.solution_text:
$71>67>64$
Maths has the highest median mark, $71$, so students did best in maths according to this measure.

$16<30<38$
Science has the smallest range, $16$, so students' science marks were most similar.

examples.question_text:
The table summarises the times taken by four age groups to complete a puzzle.

$\begin{array}{lcc}\textbf{Age (years)}&\textbf{Mean (seconds)}&\textbf{Range (seconds)}\\\hline12\text{–}16&28&19\\16\text{–}30&22&15\\30\text{–}60&34&24\\\text{Over }60&46&12\end{array}$

Asha says the over $60$s did best because their mean is greatest. Explain her mistake, identify the fastest group on average, and order the groups from most consistent to least consistent.
examples.solution_text:
A lower completion time means finishing faster. The over $60$s took the longest on average, with a mean of $46$ seconds.

The $16$–$30$ group was fastest on average, with the lowest mean of $22$ seconds.

$12<15<19<24$
A smaller range means greater consistency. From most consistent to least consistent: over $60$, $16$–$30$, $12$–$16$, $30$–$60$.

examples.question_text:
Two groups completed the same test. Their completion times are summarised below.

$\begin{array}{lccc}\textbf{Group}&\textbf{Mean (minutes)}&\textbf{Median (minutes)}&\textbf{Range (minutes)}\\\hline\text{A}&32.4&32.0&7.5\\\text{B}&30.8&30.5&10.2\end{array}$

Compare the groups' completion times using the mean, median and range.
examples.solution_text:
$30.8<32.4$ and $30.5<32.0$
Group B finished faster on average: both its mean and median completion times are lower.

$7.5<10.2$
Group A's completion times were more consistent because its range is smaller.

Group B was faster on average, while Group A was more consistent.

examples.question_text:
A school wants to find out whether its $720$ students would attend an after-school music concert. All $26$ members of the school band are surveyed, and $21$ say yes.

The organiser concludes that most students at the school would attend. Explain why this conclusion may be invalid, and state what the responses do show.
examples.solution_text:
Only school band members were surveyed. They may be more interested in a music concert than other students, whose preferences were not collected.

The responses show that $21$ of the $26$ band members surveyed would attend. They do not establish that most of the school's $720$ students would attend.

examples.question_text:
A teacher introduces a two-week spelling programme. The class's test results before and after the programme are summarised below.

$\begin{array}{lccc}&\textbf{Lowest mark}&\textbf{Mean mark}&\textbf{Highest mark}\\\hline\text{Before}&4&11.5&18\\\text{After}&8&14&20\end{array}$

The teacher concludes that the programme caused the improvement. What improvement does the table show? Explain why the table alone does not establish the cause, and suggest a fair-test comparison.
examples.solution_text:
$14>11.5$
The class's mean mark increased from $11.5$ to $14$, so the class scored higher on average after the programme.

The change alone does not establish that the programme caused the improvement. Other differences, such as test difficulty or additional practice, could have affected the results.

Compare the change with a similar control group that does not receive the programme, using tests of comparable difficulty and keeping other conditions as similar as possible.

coverage.summary: Authored six examples covering the distinct assessed methods with changed values and booklet-supported reasoning. Prompts and solutions are separate editable fields; solution prose and mathematics inherit the renderer's blue. Independent comparisons need no phantom equals gutters, and these tasks require no diagrams. Retained assessments were used only for method classification and were neither altered nor re-audited. Independent example review and actual rendering verification remain subsequent stages.

examples.derivation: 53 > 46, so Theo scored more on average. 18 < 31, so Amira was more consistent. Neither leads on both measures. This follows the source cricket comparison.
71 > 67 > 64 identifies maths as having the highest median. 16 < 30 < 38 identifies science as having the smallest spread. This matches the source subject-table method.
22 < 28 < 34 < 46, so ages 16–30 were fastest on average and over 60s were slowest. Ordering ranges 12 < 15 < 19 < 24 gives over 60, 16–30, 12–16, 30–60 from most to least consistent.

Group B has both the lower mean, 30.8 < 32.4, and lower median, 30.5 < 32.0, supporting faster typical completion. Group A has the smaller range, 7.5 < 10.2, supporting greater consistency. The source teaches comparing these three statistics for completion times.

The survey covers all 26 band members but excludes the other 694 students. Band members may have different interest in a music concert. The 21 yes responses establish a majority within the band, without establishing a school-wide majority. This follows the source restricted-group sampling reasoning.

The mean increased by 14 − 11.5 = 2.5 marks, supporting higher scores on average after the programme. Before-and-after results alone do not isolate its effect. Comparing changes with a similar untreated control group under comparable testing conditions follows the source fair-test method.

review.summary: All six examples are correct, source-supported and within scope. All 19 exact assessment locators are mapped, and every distinct assessed method has example coverage. No existing examples or source exceptions require review. Separate editable fields and single-dollar mathematics comply; independent comparisons need no phantom equals gutters. Tables provide sufficient information without additional diagrams. Solution prose and mathematics inherit blue from the confirmed renderer. Actual rendering verification remains a later stage. Accepted assessment mathematics was not re-audited.
